changes.text: 一九一五到一九一七年，一个自称保守、认为语言文字最不易变的中国留学生，按他自述，是被一张传单、几首打油诗和朋友的反对，一步步推到只用白话作诗的决定上。他把主张写得温和，《新青年》主编陈独秀却替他把旗子举高成“革命”。

Between 1915 and 1917, a Chinese student in America who called himself a conservative — who thought language and writing the world's most unchanging things — was, by his own account, pushed by a leaflet, a few doggerel verses and his friends' opposition into writing poetry in the spoken language alone. He worded his claim modestly; Chen Duxiu, editor of New Youth, raised the banner for him, into "revolution."
一九一六年七月底八月初，在美国留学的胡适给自己定了一条规矩：不再写旧诗词，只用白话作诗；诗集名字他都想好了，叫《尝试集》。可他一向说自己是保守的人，认为语言文字是世界上最保守的东西，比宗教还保守，还说这一路是被「逼上梁山」的——这句成语说的是一个人为环境所迫，不得已而做出违反他本意的非常行为。

In late July and early August of 1916, Hu Shi, a Chinese student in America, gave himself a rule: no more old-style verse. He would write poetry only in baihua, the everyday spoken language, and he had already named the book to come — Changshi ji, "Experiments." Yet he called himself a conservative: language and writing, he liked to say, are the most conservative things in the world, more conservative than religion. He had been pushed here — bi shang Liangshan, "driven to Liangshan," an idiom for someone forced by circumstances into extraordinary acts against his own intentions.
按他自己的说法，把他推到这一步的，不是什么大事件，而是一首送别诗引起的小小偶然事件，和朋友之间持续一年多的争吵。争的是白话能不能用来写文学：到一九一六年夏天，朋友们已承认白话可以写小说、演说，唯独不肯承认它能作诗——反对者已经退到只剩一处：诗。

In his own telling, what pushed him was no great event, but a small accident set off by a farewell poem, and a quarrel among friends that ran on for over a year. The quarrel was over whether the vernacular could serve literature. By the summer of 1916 his friends granted it would do for fiction and speeches, but not for poetry. Poetry was the last fortress.

更早的引子，藏在每月的支票信封里。庚款留学生每月从华盛顿的清华学生监督处收到一张支票，主办的书记钟文鳌——一位教会学校出身、热心改革社会风俗的好好先生——总在信封里夹一张小传单，上面写着「不满二十五岁不娶妻。」「废除汉字，改用字母！」「多种树，种树有益。」之类的话。平时大家随手把它丢进纸篓。约在一九一五年，胡适却坐下来回了一张很不客气的字条，大意是：像你这样既不懂汉字、又不能写汉文的人，「你最好闭起鸟嘴！」

The first trigger hid in a monthly check. Chinese students on the Boxer Indemnity scholarship drew their stipend from the Tsinghua student-supervision office in Washington, and inside every envelope was a leaflet slipped in by the clerk who mailed it: Zhong Wen'ao, a kindly man from the missionary school St. John's in Shanghai, who was keen to reform Chinese society. Its slogans ran, in translation: marry no one under twenty-five; abolish the Chinese characters and switch to an alphabet; plant more trees, for trees do good. Usually it went straight into the wastebasket. Around 1915 Hu sat down and wrote back a rude little note, which ran roughly, in translation: a man like you, who neither understands the characters nor can write the language, had better shut his beak.

字条寄出后他心中懊悔，觉得不该对一位和善又有心改革语言文字的人如此不礼貌，于是在朋友面前自我谴责，并想到一层：假如钟君这样的人不够资格谈这个问题，那么够资格的人实在更该认真研究，把可行与不可行的问题都摆出来检讨。他找上一九一〇年同进康乃尔的赵元任，两人商定把“中国文字的问题”作为美东中国学生会文学股年会的论题，各写一篇：赵元任论吾国文字能否采用字母制及其进行方法，他论“如何可使吾国文言易于教授”。

After the note was sent, he regretted it. Zhong was a kind man with a sincere wish to reform Chinese customs and writing; the rudeness was uncalled for, and Hu reproached himself before his friends. Then a further thought: if men like Zhong are not qualified to discuss such questions, then the qualified should do the work — set out what is feasible and what is not, and examine both. He took it up with Zhao Yuanren, who had entered Cornell with him in 1910. They agreed to make "the question of China's writing" the literature section's topic for the annual meeting of the Chinese Students' Association in the East, and split it: Zhao on whether the Chinese script could adopt an alphabetic system and how to proceed; Hu on "how to make our classical written language easier to teach."
一年多，一场争论
A Year and More of Argument

争论是从一首送别诗开始的。胡适准备离开康乃尔时，朋友梅光迪在绮色佳度假，正要去哈佛跟白璧德深造；梅光迪也是庚款留学生，此前在威斯康辛大学读完英国文学学士学位。胡适写了首相当长的打油诗送行，里面塞进十一个外国人的名字，从爱默生、达尔文到牛顿、爱迪生。在康乃尔的任鸿隽把这些名字连缀起来，作诗嘲笑他「文学今革命，作诗送胡生！」。胡适自认那首送行诗立意严肃：诗里鼓励朋友们留意今后中国文学的发展，并说致力于中国文学革命，贡献不下于征服自然，他叫它作「缩地戡天」。所以他不肯轻轻放过，在从绮色佳去纽约的火车上作答诗，第一次写下“诗国革命”的念头：「诗国革命何自始？要须作诗如作文！」

It began with a farewell poem. When Hu was preparing to leave Cornell, his friend Mei Guangdi — a Boxer Indemnity scholar with a bachelor's in English literature from Wisconsin — was on holiday in Ithaca before going on to Harvard to study under the critic Irving Babbitt. Hu sent him off with a doggerel poem, long by Chinese standards, stuffed with eleven foreign names — Emerson, Darwin, Newton, Edison and the rest. Another Cornell friend, Ren Hongjun, strung the names into a mock verse of his own, which in our translation runs: literature's revolution today, a poem to send off Hu. Hu would not let it pass. His send-off had been meant in earnest, urging friends to watch where Chinese literature went next and ranking its revolution with conquering nature — what he called, in our translation, shrinking the earth and taming the heavens. So on the train from Ithaca to New York he wrote an answer, and in it first set down the idea of a revolution in the poetry world. His couplet, in our translation, asks where that revolution should begin, and answers that poetry must be written like prose.
一九一六年七月六日，他在日记里写下九条主张，头两条是「今日之文言乃是一种半死的文字。」和「今日之白话是一种活的语言。」他说这九条很确切地表达了他策动中国文学革命的中心思想；又说这许多严肃的讨论和历史性的研析，其实都只源于一首送别诗引起的小小偶然事件。

Then the diary. On July 6, 1916, he set down nine propositions; the first two, in translation: the classical written language of today is a half-dead form of writing; the vernacular of today is a living language. These nine, he said, expressed precisely the central ideas behind his launching of China's literary revolution — and all these serious discussions and historical analyses came out of one small accident, a farewell poem to a friend going to Harvard.

两天之后，凯约嘉湖上出了桩险事。七月八日，任鸿隽、陈衡哲、梅光迪、杨铨、唐钺等人在湖上划船，忽然风暴骤起，雨落下来，他们急忙往岸边划，几乎把船弄翻，上岸时个个狼狈。任鸿隽随后写了一首四言古诗《泛湖即事》附在信里，请胡适批评。诗中用了“言”一类的老字，而胡适此前恰好写过一篇《言字解》。他不喜欢这种陈腐文字与现代语言夹杂，回信说此诗“文字殊不调和”，用的是「三千年前之死语」。任鸿隽不服，愤愤不平；更有意思的是梅光迪路见不平，写来一封十分激动的信反击。梅当时正受保守派批评家白璧德的影响，坚持文学的文字、尤其是诗的文字，必须由第一流的诗人和美术家加以锻炼美化。

Two days later, another accident. On July 8 Ren Hongjun, Chen Hengzhe of Vassar, Mei Guangdi, Yang Quan, Tang Yue and others were rowing on Cayuga Lake when a black cloud gathered overhead, a storm broke and the rain fell; pulling for shore in a hurry they nearly capsized, and climbed out soaked and dishevelled. For that band of students it was a real adventure, and Ren wrote it up in "On the Lake," an old four-character-style poem he mailed to Hu for criticism. It used archaic words such as the particle yan, of the kind found in the Book of Songs — Hu had earlier written an essay on that very word — and he disliked dead diction mixed with modern language. He wrote back that the poem was bad because its wording was thoroughly incongruous, and he spoke of dead language of three thousand years ago (both paraphrased from the Chinese). Ren was indignant. More interesting was the letter that followed: Mei at Harvard, riding to the rescue in high dudgeon. Under the influence of his conservative teacher Babbitt, Mei opposed Hu all the way — language becomes poetic only after first-rate poets refine it, and the language of literature, poetry above all, must be beautified by first-rate poets and artists before it counts as poetic diction. On that ground he lashed Hu's ideas.

胡适的回应是一首约一百句的滑稽打油诗，他生平写的最长的一首：开头描写老梅大发脾气，再举许多例子开玩笑地驳“文字哪有死活”，并顺着对方的论点反将一军——文字须经诗人长期锻炼，这正是他想做的事，当代的诗人作家正该把这些俗语俗字锻炼起来，提高它们的地位。两位朋友读了大发雷霆，复信取笑他，但信里有一个共同的让步：白话可用在评话、故事、小说、演说上，唯独不能用在诗里。任鸿隽说得最干脆：「白话自有白话用处（如作小说、演说等），然不能用之于诗！」

Hu answered with a comic doggerel poem of about a hundred lines, the longest he ever wrote: Old Mei in a towering rage, examples piled up to mock the theory that words have no life or death, and Mei's own argument turned against him — if words must be forged by poets over long practice, that is exactly what he wanted. Contemporary poets and writers should take these vulgar, colloquial words, temper them, raise their standing and bring them into poetry. The burlesque threw both friends into a fury; both wrote back to mock his vernacular verse, yet their letters shared a concession: the vernacular would do for storytelling, fiction, novels and speeches — everything except poetry. Ren was bluntest; his letter said, in translation, that the vernacular has its own uses, such as novels and speeches, but cannot be used for poetry.

七月底，他写信告诉这些朋友：白话也可以作诗，以往白话诗不多，今后可以多写，当务之急是自己认真着实地试验。七月二十六日他写信给任鸿隽，说「文字者，文学之器也」，文言决不足为吾国将来文学之利器，施耐庵、曹雪芹已经实地证明作小说之利器在于白话，「今尚需人实地试验白话是否可为韵文之利器耳」。他把这件事比作开辟新地：「我此时练习白话诗文，颇似新辟一文学殖民地」，可惜须单身匹马前往，难得同志结伴。信里也写到失败的可能：新开之地若尽是不毛之土，自己终归老于“文言诗国”也说不定；若侥幸有成，辟除荆棘之后自会开放门户，迎朋友同来。七月底八月初，他决定不再写旧诗词，专写白话诗，并在写出几首之前就给下一个诗集定名《尝试集》。

In late July he wrote to these friends that the vernacular could be poetry: little had been written before, but more could be written now, in every colour and shape, and the urgent task was to experiment in earnest. On July 26 he wrote Ren — paraphrased here from the Chinese — that words are the instrument of literature, that the classical language could never be the sharp instrument China's future literature needed, and that Shi Nai'an and Cao Xueqin had proved in practice that the instrument for fiction is the vernacular; what remained was for someone to test in practice whether it could be the instrument of verse. He likened his practice in vernacular poetry and prose to opening up a new literary colony; it was a pity he had to go alone, with few companions. The letter also allowed for failure: if the new land proved to be sand and barren ground, he might end his days in the kingdom of classical poetry after all; if by luck he succeeded, after clearing the brambles he would open the gates and welcome his friends in. In late July and early August he decided to stop writing old-style verse — and before he had written more than a handful of vernacular poems, he had named the next collection Experiments.

一九一六年十一月，他把一年多讨论的结果写成文章，提出八条很温和的建议，题目用的是“改良”和“刍议”。据他事后解释，“文学革命”一词在他自己的诗和信里、朋友给他的来信里早已常见，有时是开玩笑，有时也很严肃；但第一次把结论送到国内发表时，他考虑到老一辈保守分子无可怀疑的反对，刻意把文题写得温和而谦虚。文章誊了三份：一份交给他自己主编、当时由商务印书馆承印的《中国留美学生季报》，一份寄给陈独秀主编、已出版数年的《新青年》；陈独秀于一九一六年受聘为国立北京大学文科学长。

In November 1916 he shaped more than a year of argument into an article with eight very moderate suggestions. Even the title was modest: he dropped "literary revolution," a phrase that had come up often in his own poems and letters and in his friends' letters to him, sometimes in jest and sometimes in earnest. This was the first time the conclusions would be sent home to China for publication, and, in view of the undoubted resistance of the older conservatives, he kept the wording gentle — reform, not revolution; a humble opinion, not dogma. Three copies: one to the Chinese Students' Quarterly he edited in America, then printed by the Commercial Press; one to New Youth, which Chen Duxiu — from 1916 dean of arts at National Peking University — had been editing for several years.

一九一七年一月，文章在《新青年》刊出，文化界反应很大。北大有两位教授重视它：一位是陈独秀本人，本是死硬派的革命人物，随后写《文学革命论》响应，公开支持文学革命，并说首举义旗的是朋友胡适，自己高张大旗作声援；另一位是古典音韵学教授、章太炎门人钱玄同，这位古文大家没有写文章，却写去小批评大捧场的长信，也在《新青年》发表，声势为之一振。赵元任则常说胡适的白话诗文“不够白”，不是一般人常用的真正语体；胡适承认了，打了个比方：像裹了四十年或者二十年小脚的女人，纵使把小脚放大，终究恢复不了天足。

It appeared in New Youth in January 1917 and stirred a great response. Two Peking University professors took it seriously. Chen Duxiu, an unbending revolutionary, answered with "On Literary Revolution," publicly backing a literary revolution and saying frankly that the banner had been raised by his friend Hu Shi; he was only hoisting a flag in support. Qian Xuantong, professor of classical phonology, a master of ancient prose and a disciple of the great scholar Zhang Taiyan, wrote no article but sent Chen and Hu long letters — small criticisms, great praise — also printed in New Youth; that so eminent a classicist should sympathize buoyed their cause. Zhao Yuanren often said that Hu's vernacular poems and essays were "not vernacular enough," not the genuine spoken style ordinary people used. Hu admitted it: like a woman who had bound her feet for forty, or even twenty, years, however much she loosened the bindings she would never recover natural feet.
胡适自己对来龙去脉的解释是反对单因论。他开玩笑说，历史上的意外事件往往比“单因”——经济、色欲、上帝之类——更重要：正因为这些单因对所有事件皆可解释，它们也就不可解释任何事件。就他这段经历而言，传单、送别诗、湖上险些翻船都是意外；他把一连串小意外看作推力，这是他本人的史观，不是本文的结论。

Hu's own explanation of how it all happened is that he opposed single-cause theories of history. He used to joke that accidents matter more than any monistic cause — economics, lust, God and the rest: those single causes explain everything that has ever happened, and precisely because they explain everything, they explain nothing. In his own story the leaflet, the farewell poem and the near-capsize on the lake were accidents. Reading a chain of small accidents as the push behind his position is Hu's own view of history, not a finding of this article.

作者推断：他选择以身作则，并不只是姿态，而是把分歧改造成可检验的问题。“白话不能用之于诗”是个全称判断，理论上一首像样的白话诗就能动摇它；反之，没有诗，再多书信也只是意见相持。他把新诗集提前定名《尝试集》，等于当众揽下举证责任，把胜负交给一场公开、长期、别人看得见的试验。一种解释是，这也呼应了译注者唐德刚对他的定位——夹在必然与偶然之间的“实验主义者”，不肯听任事情自然演变，而要在试验中寻找方向。不过「没有“胡适”，恐怕也就没有“白话文运动”——至少运动也不会在那时就发生了」是唐德刚的评论，不是可核实的史实。

The author's inference: his decision to lead by example was not merely a pose; it converted a disagreement into a testable question. "The vernacular cannot be used for poetry" is a universal claim, and one decent vernacular poem is enough in principle to shake it; without a poem, letters could go on forever as a standoff of opinions. By naming the collection Experiments in advance, he publicly took on the burden of proof and left the outcome to a long, open trial that others could watch. One reading is that this matches the translator-editor Tang Degang's portrait of him as a pragmatist standing between necessity and chance, unwilling to let events drift and determined to search out the right direction through experiment. Still, Tang's remark — in paraphrase, that without Hu Shi there would probably have been no Vernacular Movement, or at least it would not have happened then — is commentary, not verifiable history.
另一种解释是关于措辞的分工：他把“革命”换成“改良”，把结论降格为“刍议”，自己承担温和的发表风险；陈独秀随后把它高举为“文学革命”，由更激进的人去举旗。按陈独秀的说法，举义旗的是胡适，他只是作声援。这种“一人放低、一人举高”的配合，是作者从先后次序读出的一种可能，并非本文所据材料的记载。

A second reading concerns the division of labour over words. He swapped revolution for reform and demoted his conclusion to a humble opinion, taking on himself the risk of publishing moderately; Chen Duxiu then raised it as literary revolution, and a more radical man carried the flag. On Chen's own account the banner was Hu's; he was merely coming up in support. This doubling — one man lowering the volume, one raising it — is a possibility the author reads in the sequence, not something recorded in the material this piece relies on.
结局也可以交代一笔。胡适自述，运动约四年就在学校教育上基本成功：一九二〇年北京政府教育部通令，国民小学一、二年级教材一律改用白话，旧教材分期废除。但他称之为“部分的胜利”，重要的部分是以白话为教育工具；他同时说，一九一九年的学生运动把文化运动变成了政治运动，对文艺复兴运动是一种“干扰”，虽则对传播白话文功不可没。

The outcome can be set down too. By Hu's account, in only about four years the effort to replace the classical language with the vernacular in the schools had all but succeeded: in 1920 the Ministry of Education of the Beijing government ordered that all first- and second-year textbooks in the national primary schools be written entirely in the vernacular, with the old textbooks abolished in stages. Yet he called it only a partial victory; the important part was making the vernacular the instrument of education. He also said the student movement of 1919 had been an interruption to the Renaissance movement, turning a cultural movement into a political one, though it did much to spread the vernacular.
第二件事是措辞。你把方案叫做“优化”，心里想的是换掉整套流程；这时有人替你把它命名为“流程革命”，还抄送了全员。要不要接？胡适自己的文章用了温和的词，后来是陈独秀把它举成“革命”。接住响亮说法的好处是声量大，代价是解释权易手，而被温和措辞吸引来的中间派，可能被激进的命名吓退。这是作者提出的取舍，并非只有这一种做法。

The second thing is wording. You call your plan an optimization while meaning to replace the whole process; someone else renames it a process revolution and copies the whole company. Do you accept the label? Hu's own article used moderate words; it was Chen Duxiu who later raised it as a revolution. Taking the ringing phrase buys attention; the cost is losing control of the definition, and the middle-of-the-road people drawn in by gentle wording may be scared off by a radical name. This is the trade-off the author offers; it is not the only way.
本文材料只来自一本书：胡适口述、唐德刚译注《胡适口述自传》（中国文史出版社2020年）。按唐德刚说明，这一章英文稿是从《四十自述》中《逼上梁山》一节节译、经胡适手订后又回译成中文的，与原文多少有点出入。因此这是当事人多年后的自述，不是当时的独立记录；梅光迪、任鸿隽的反应和话语，都经胡适转述，本文不推测他们的内心。

The material here comes from one book only: Hu Shi's oral memoir, translated and annotated by Tang Degang, The Oral Memoir of Hu Shi (Chinese Literature and History Press, 2020). As Tang explains, the English draft of this chapter was abridged from the "Driven to Liangshan" section of Hu's Forty Self-Narratives, revised in Hu's own hand, then translated back into Chinese — and it differs from the original in some degree. This is therefore a participant's account given many years later, not an independent record from the time. Mei Guangdi's and Ren Hongjun's reactions and their words all reach us through Hu's retelling, and this piece does not speculate about their inner thoughts.

几处需要降级看待：他为何用“改良”不用“革命”，是本人事后的解释；唐德刚关于“实验主义者”“鸡蛋与鸡，必然和偶然是说不清的”等说法，都是译注者的评论；对“文言是半死的文字”这句口号，唐德刚认为它当年有摧枯拉朽的功能，但真实性值得重新商榷。白话文与白话诗的结局也不同：按唐德刚的说法，白话文是百分之百成功，白话诗则未必——至少还未脱离“尝试”阶段。文中主要日期依据本书：约一九一五年（胡适说“我想是”）、一九一六年二三月、三月、七月六日、七月八日、七月二十六日、七月底八月初、十一月、一九一七年一月。

A few things should be read with lowered confidence. Why he used reform rather than revolution is his own retrospective explanation. Tang Degang's remarks about the pragmatist and about the chicken and the egg — necessity and chance are impossible to disentangle — are the annotator's commentary, not fact. On the slogan that the classical language is a half-dead form of writing, Tang thought it had a devastating force in its day but that its truth is worth debating again. The two outcomes also differ: in Tang's judgment vernacular prose was a hundred per cent successful, while vernacular poetry was not necessarily so — at least it has not yet left the experimental stage. The main dates used here follow the book: around 1915 (Hu's own "I think it was"); February and March 1916; March 1916; July 6; July 8; July 26; late July and early August; November 1916; January 1917.
还有两点作者的补白：文中说小说年代“元明之辨”的修正，来自胡适本人晚年的更正，本文只依据这一更正，未另行核验；至于“若无胡适则运动不会发生”这类反事实，只能当作唐德刚的看法，作者不作结论，也不替历史排演它没有走过的路。

Two further notes from the author. The correction over the dating of the novels — Yuan versus Ming — comes from Hu's own later recantation; this piece relies on that correction alone and has not checked it further. And counterfactuals of the sort "without Hu Shi the movement would not have happened" can only be treated as Tang Degang's opinion; the author draws no conclusion, and does not rehearse roads history did not take.
